# Predicting Boundary Points of Combinatorics-Retaining Domains Generated by the Mean-Median Map Using Machine-Learning Models

**Justin Ryan Pangestu, Jonathan Hoseana, Robyn Irawan**
Center for Mathematics and Society, Faculty of Science,
Parahyangan Catholic University (UNPAR), Bandung, West Java, Indonesia
<robynirawan.tjia@unpar.ac.id>

[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.21952439.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21952439)

---

## Overview

This repository contains the complete pipeline for the study reported in:

> Pangestu, J. R., Hoseana, J., Irawan, R. Predicting Boundary Points of Combinatorics-Retaining Domains Generated by the Mean-Median Map Using Machine-Learning Models. *Computational Statistics* (in preparation).

The study investigates whether machine-learning models can predict whether a given rational number is a boundary point of a *combinatorics-retaining domain* generated by the mean-median map, based on numerical quantities describing the dynamical behaviour of the corresponding orbit. A dataset of 6,818 rational numbers is generated using the method of Cellarosi and Munday (2016), and three models — logistic regression (with AIC-based stepwise selection), a decision tree, and a random forest — are fitted and compared on held-out training, validation, and testing splits. A robustness check further verifies that predictive performance is not primarily driven by a dataset-construction artefact tied to denominator size.

## Repository Contents

```
mean-median-map-ml/
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── .gitignore
├── data/
│   └── mean_median_dataset.csv        # 6,818 rational numbers x 12 predictor variables + target
├── code/
│   ├── 01_dataset_generation.mw       # Maple worksheet: generates the dataset via the
│   │                                  #   Cellarosi-Munday combinatorics-retaining-domain algorithm
│   ├── 02_logistic_regression.Rmd     # LR model, AIC-based stepwise selection, ROC/AUC
│   ├── 03_decision_tree.Rmd           # Decision tree model, parameter grid search, ROC/AUC
│   ├── 04_random_forest.Rmd           # Random forest model, OOB-based parameter selection,
│   │                                  #   mean-decrease-in-accuracy / mean-decrease-in-Gini
│   └── 05_robustness_check.Rmd        # Refits LR/DT/RF after excluding X1, and after excluding
│                                      #   X1 and X3, to check whether predictive performance
│                                      #   depends on the denominator-construction artefact;
│                                      #   also reports a trivial denominator-threshold baseline
└── outputs/
    └── robustness_check_results.csv   # Accuracy/Precision/Recall/F-Score/AUC for every
                                       #   model x predictor-set combination in 05, plus baseline
```

`data/mean_median_dataset.csv` is the dataset used throughout the paper — running the R scripts does not require re-running the Maple worksheet.

## How to Run

1. Clone or download this repository.
2. Open `code/02_logistic_regression.Rmd`, `code/03_decision_tree.Rmd`, and `code/04_random_forest.Rmd` in RStudio.
3. Set the working directory to the project root (Session → Set Working Directory → To Source File Location), or edit the data-loading path at the top of each script to point at `data/mean_median_dataset.csv`.
4. Knit or run each `.Rmd` independently — each script loads the dataset, performs the 70/10/20 train/validation/test split, fits its model, and reports Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F-Score, and AUC.
5. (Optional) Open `code/01_dataset_generation.mw` in Maple to inspect or re-run the dataset-generation algorithm.
6. (Optional) Knit `code/05_robustness_check.Rmd` to reproduce the robustness check reported in the paper — it saves its results to `outputs/robustness_check_results.csv` and produces ROC comparison plots for each model.

---

## Dataset

Each row is a rational number $r_i \in [1/2, 2/3]$ together with 12 predictor variables computed from the orbit of $[0, r_i, 1]$ under the mean-median map (denominator/numerator of $r_i$, denominator/numerator of the orbit's limit, transit time, repeat time, denominator/numerator of the largest orbit term, number of terms below the limit, number of increases, denominator/numerator of the maximum consecutive difference), and a binary target indicating whether $r_i$ is a boundary point of a combinatorics-retaining domain. Full variable definitions are given in the manuscript.
